# Standing Up for Half Moon Bay
## Half Moon Bay is a little slice of paradise,
and I want to make sure it stays that way.
We need to grow with intent and purpose.
# The Short List
There’s a lot to be done in the city of Half Moon Bay,
and there’s a lot to be done in our district (District 1)
### Citywide
Protect Measure D (our 1½% growth per year limit) from the state of California
Fight for public hearings for all major building projects in HMB
Make HMB more affordable
Establish local preference for local housing projects – they’re for people in HMB, not for Menlo Park or Burlingame
Set up a live-work initiative so people working here can find housing
Support a public swimming pool
Establish urgent care services on the coast
Balance the budget – no structural deficit every year!
Help downtown businesses thrive, create gateway to downtown
Finish trail system east of Hwy 1
Protect the look and feel of Half Moon Bay – keep it neighborly and beautiful
Replant the medians along Hwy. 1
Address the high-fire risk and lack of evacuation procedures
Be more cost-conscious about City Attorney time at public and staff meetings
### District 1
Bike route and walking trail on the east side of Hwy 1 needs to extend north to El Granada and south to Main Street
Initiate CDP process to thin out the brush inside Frenchman’s Creek, to minimize fire risk and address takeover by invasive species
Help neighborhoods plan for emergencies
Address fire risk
Make Hwy 1 safer and keep traffic moving
Explore David's Priorities →
## Who the heck is
David Gorn?
David has lived in the Frenchman's Creek area for nearly 30 years and is raising his two children on the Coastside. He has served six years on the Half Moon Bay Planning Commission, worked with local nonprofits including Coastside Children's Programs and Coastal Lit, supported school parcel tax initiatives, hosted a local news podcast, and previously served as editor of the Half Moon Bay Review.
# Why I’m Running
We are facing the most important time in Half Moon Bay in the past 20 years.
Half Moon Bay needs affordable housing and thoughtful growth — but residents should have a meaningful voice in how major projects are developed.
# Three Big Priorities
### Urgent Care on the Coast
The Coastside does not have urgent care services. Crazy. And in the event of road closures (earthquake, wildfire, etc), we could be isolated for an extended time. That’s big trouble. I have a plan I think can work.
### A Public Swimming Pool
The Coastside has discussed a community pool for decades. We are SO close to a public pool; the school district already approved it. It’s time to get it across the finish line.
### A Thriving Downtown
Improve gateway signage to direct visitors downtown, improve parking, walkability and cleanliness to supporting the businesses that make downtown Main Street special.
# …And Five More
#### Wildfire risk,
insurance and evacuation planning
#### Replant the medians
along Hwy 1
#### Complete the bike and pedestrian
trail east of Hwy 1
#### Encourage infill housing
and ADUs
#### Make sure building projects include public hearings and input
# 555 Kelly
Sure, lots of other things need attention in Half Moon Bay, but everyone wants to talk about 555 Kelly, so let’s talk about it.
I believe that project was so contentious because the citizens of Half Moon Bay were not heard. Because of something called the Super Density Bonus Law, city officials and citizens were not able to raise questions and ask for compromises over issues like parking and traffic and 5-story building height and public safety — and when people’s concerns are ignored or dismissed, they get angry. If 555 Kelly had gone through the normal process, those questions of height and parking and so on would have been addressed, there would have been some small compromises and the same approval timeline would have been met. The project applicants decided to go along a different path, one of confrontation, deception, and shaming. It’s too bad. Every other affordable housing project in this town has been embraced. But forcing this project through without engaging the questions about it, that just resulted in rancor and ill feeling.
A couple of other important things: That lack of public input is on display again in the 940 Main project, also known as the Metzgar project. This time the applicant invoked something called “by-right process,” and “ministerial approval.” That means no public hearings. No City Council input, no Planning Commission input, no public input.
Just to be clear, there is a reason why Half Moon Bay has already built a lot of affordable housing on its own, without prodding by the state — many of our citizens can’t afford to live here. We’re not a rich community, and affordable housing projects have been not only accepted but encouraged here. And the 940 Main project has a developer, MidPen, with a good track record. The project looks appealing. However…
This dynamic of no public input sets a dangerous precedent. The state of California decided to bully Half Moon Bay and they got what they wanted — two housing projects where public input and project compromise is minimal. When a bully gets his way, he doesn’t suddenly become your friend. A bully comes back and wants more. My concern is that this dynamic will repeat itself with bigger projects. Hey, if you have 20% affordable housing, you can build whatever else you want — hotel, conference center, five stories tall, luxury homes, etc. — with no input from anyone who lives in Half Moon Bay. That is in our future, if we let it.
Two quick asides — sorry to go on, but it’s important:
## #1
The state of California has singled out little Half Moon Bay as the poster child for its housing push. Are we recalcitrant NIMBYs who don’t like affordable housing? That just doesn’t track. We have been building affordable housing long before the state decided to push. As a community, we built Lesley Gardens senior housing, Main Street affordable housing, Stone Pine Cove farmworker housing, Half Moon Village senior housing. Moonridge Housing was a county project, but all of these major housing projects were proposed, approved and built with little resistance. There is no NIMBYism here. We are a town of modest incomes and modest means, and we understand the need for affordable housing and we have embraced it in our town.
## #2
## #3
A lot of the housing we’ve already built has been for others. Lesley Gardens was supposed to address the dire need for low-income seniors here in Half Moon Bay. But those housing units went predominantly to the rest of the county and beyond — and we STILL have low-income seniors here who can’t afford to live here.
Measure D is our voter-approved 1 1/2% growth limit, prompted by concerns of a lack of infrastructure — like our extremely limited water supply, and our roads already packed with cars. The state housing agency petitioned the Coastal Commission to rescind Measure D. Then tried to get HMB City Council to put it on the ballot, said voters should rescind it. Why rescind it? Well, California’s housing agency has big plans for Half Moon Bay, far beyond 555 Kelly and the Metzgar project.
»»»» Since I first wrote this, three new housing projects have been proposed for HMB: 370 homes at the Podesta property below the high school; 125 units at a site just south of Rocket Farms; additionally another 99 units at Rocket Farm. That’s almost 600 more homes, 1,200 more cars, who knows where the water comes from… Are you not too worried if the state gets rid of Measure D? Might be time to start worrying.
We need a Local Preference ordinance so that, when we build more affordable housing, the citizens living here get a chance at living there.
(When we approved and built Lesley Gardens senior housing, for instance, the community at the time saw that many seniors couldn’t afford to live here — but that project was not predominantly for local residents, it was predominantly for seniors from other areas of the county and state. So Half Moon Bay still has a problem, where our seniors can’t afford to stay here.)
I also think a Live/Work ordinance makes sense — so the people who work here and commute in from other places like Daly City also get a chance at housing. Living near your work cuts down on traffic and pollution, and fosters that sense of neighborliness we all love.
# What I'm Hearing
“We need speed bumps. We have small children in this neigborhood.”
"What happened to the suicide lane outside Grandview during the repaving?”
“When will the eastside trail ever go from HMB to El Granada?”
"I cannot make that left turn onto Hwy 1. What can we do?"
“What happened to our school buses? Buses would get a lot of cars off the road.”
“Why is there no streetlight in the first block of Grandview?”
“Why does the Frenchman's Creek traffic light take so long?"
"School teams should be free. Why does the public school make families pay for school sports?"
David wants to hear from you!
